title: Rigveda 8.81: To Indra
source: Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 (undated (catalogued with Penn's 18th-19th c. Vedic manuscripts)), OPenn, Public Domain Mark + Aufrecht's accented text (GRETIL) + Griffith's English (VedaWeb)
description: Rigveda 8.81: To Indra: Sanskrit text and Griffith's English, each verse linked to the page of an undated Rigveda manuscript (Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41) that carries it.
introduction:
Rigveda 8.81 is a hymn of 9 verses addressed to Indra. It stands in book (maṇḍala) 8, the book of the Kaṇva and Aṅgiras poets. The Rigveda is the oldest collection of Sanskrit hymns, composed in the second half of the second millennium BCE and handed down orally for many centuries before it was written down.

The manuscript shown is Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 (University of Pennsylvania), an undated paper manuscript of the padapāṭha (the word-by-word recitation text, in which every word is written separately and compounds are split) of the whole Ṛgveda in Devanāgarī, 884 leaves in fascicles, 7-9 lines to the page, accents in red; this hymn stands on fol. 648v. Each section below gives the verses that end on one page; the page boundaries were read on the images (the opening words of every page), not counted out. Where the manuscript is a padapāṭha (the word-by-word recitation text), the section shows Aufrecht's continuous (saṃhitā) text first and, as the edition text, the padapāṭha of the same verses, which is the form written on the page.
translator_notes: Sanskrit: Aufrecht's edition (1877) with the Vedic accents, as entered by van Nooten and Holland (GRETIL).

English: Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda (1889-1892; 2nd ed. 1896-1897), from the VedaWeb digital text; OCR slips in that text were corrected against the printed 2nd edition (data/sources/rigveda/griffith_errata.json).
Padapāṭha (edition text): Sansknet e-text via GRETIL (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

translation.original_ref: RV 8.81.1-9 (aṣṭaka 6, adhyāya 5, varga 37); Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41 fol. 648v
translation.original_text:
1ā tū na̍ indra kṣu̱manta̍ṁ ci̱traṁ grā̱bhaṁ saṁ gṛ̍bhāya | ma̱hā̱ha̱stī dakṣi̍ṇena ||
2vi̱dmā hi tvā̍ tuvikū̱rmiṁ tu̱vide̍ṣṇaṁ tu̱vīma̍gham | tu̱vi̱mā̱tram avo̍bhiḥ ||
3na̱hi tvā̍ śūra de̱vā na martā̍so̱ ditsa̍ntam | bhī̱maṁ na gāṁ vā̱raya̍nte ||
4eto̱ nv indra̱ṁ stavā̱meśā̍na̱ṁ vasva̍ḥ sva̱rāja̍m | na rādha̍sā mardhiṣan naḥ ||
5pra sto̍ṣa̱d upa̍ gāsiṣa̱c chrava̱t sāma̍ gī̱yamā̍nam | a̱bhi rādha̍sā jugurat ||
6ā no̍ bhara̱ dakṣi̍ṇenā̱bhi sa̱vyena̱ pra mṛ̍śa | indra̱ mā no̱ vaso̱r nir bhā̍k ||
7upa̍ krama̱svā bha̍ra dhṛṣa̱tā dhṛ̍ṣṇo̱ janā̍nām | adā̍śūṣṭarasya̱ veda̍ḥ ||
8indra̱ ya u̱ nu te̱ asti̱ vājo̱ vipre̍bhi̱ḥ sani̍tvaḥ | a̱smābhi̱ḥ su taṁ sa̍nuhi ||
9sa̱dyo̱juva̍s te̱ vājā̍ a̱smabhya̍ṁ vi̱śvaśca̍ndrāḥ | vaśai̍ś ca ma̱kṣū ja̍rante ||
translation.text:
1INDRA, God of the mighty arm, gather for us with thy right hand Manifold and nutritious spoil.
2We know thee mighty in thy deeds, of mighty bounty, mighty wealth, Mighty in measure, prompt to aid.
3Hero, when thou art fain to give, neither may Gods nor mortal men Restrain thee like a fearful Bull.
4Come, let us glorify Indra, Lord supreme of wealth, Self-ruling King: In bounty may he harm us not.
5Let prelude sound and following chant so let him hear the Sâman sung, And with his bounty answer us.
6O Indra, with thy right hand bring, and with thy left remember us. Let us not lose our share of wealth.
7Come nigh, O Bold One, boldly bring hither the riches of the churl Who giveth least of all the folk.
8Indra, the booty which thou hast with holy singers to receive, Even that booty win with us.
9Indra, thy swiftly-coming spoil, the booty which rejoices all, Sounds quick in concert with our hopes.
translation.scan_note: Penn Ms. Coll. 390 Item 41, fol. 648v (numbered 70v by the scribe) (OPenn image 649, upper leaf). Checked on the image: the Rigveda text on this page begins in RV 8.80.10 ‹-avīvṛdhat vaḥ amṛtāḥ amandīt›. The next page with Rigveda text, fol. 649r (numbered 71r by the scribe), begins in RV 8.82.1 ‹ā pra drava parāvataḥ›. Verses 8.81.1-9 end on this page.
